topic: the concept of a molecule's shape affecting its properties (VSEPR basics)

easy.text: What does VSEPR theory help predict about a molecule?

options.feedback: Correct -- VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on electron pair repulsion around a central atom.
Color isn't what VSEPR theory predicts -- it's specifically about molecular geometry/shape.
While shape can influence melting point indirectly, VSEPR itself directly predicts shape, not melting point specifically.
Radioactivity relates to nuclear stability, unrelated to VSEPR's focus on molecular shape.

medium.text: According to VSEPR theory, why do electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible?

options.text: Because electron pairs repel each other (like charges), so they naturally position themselves to minimize this repulsion
options.feedback: Correct -- this repulsion-minimizing arrangement is the core principle behind VSEPR theory.

options.text: Because electron pairs are strongly attracted to each other
options.feedback: This is backwards -- like-charged electron pairs actually REPEL each other, which is exactly why they spread apart.

options.text: Because the central atom pushes them into a random arrangement
options.feedback: The arrangement isn't random -- it specifically minimizes repulsion between the negatively charged electron pairs.

options.text: Electron pairs actually don't have any specific arrangement at all
options.feedback: Electron pairs do adopt predictable arrangements based on minimizing repulsion, which is exactly what VSEPR theory describes and predicts.

hard.text: Water (H₂O) has a bent molecular shape, not a straight line, even though it only has two hydrogen atoms attached to the central oxygen. Why does VSEPR theory predict this bent shape?

options.text: Oxygen has two additional lone (non-bonding) electron pairs that also repel the bonding pairs, pushing the hydrogen atoms into a bent arrangement rather than a straight line
options.feedback: Correct -- these lone pairs take up space and exert repulsive force just like bonding pairs, significantly affecting the final molecular shape.

options.text: Water molecules have no lone electron pairs at all
options.feedback: Water's oxygen atom actually does have two lone pairs, and these are exactly what cause the bent shape according to VSEPR theory.

options.text: The bent shape is completely random with no underlying explanation
options.feedback: The bent shape has a clear, predictable explanation rooted in VSEPR theory and the repulsion caused by oxygen's lone electron pairs.

options.text: Hydrogen atoms always repel each other strongly, regardless of the central atom
options.feedback: The bent shape is primarily explained by the CENTRAL ATOM's lone pairs (oxygen's, in this case), not a general hydrogen-hydrogen repulsion effect.

easy.hard: This theory forecasts the overall spatial arrangement of atoms bonded to a central atom.
easy.medium: This theory predicts what shape a molecule will take based on its electron arrangement.
easy.easy: This theory predicts the 3D shape of a molecule.

medium.hard: Since electron pairs carry the same type of charge, they push away from each other, seeking the most spread-out possible arrangement.
medium.medium: Since electron pairs all have the same negative charge, they push each other as far apart as possible.
medium.easy: Since electron pairs all have the same charge, they push each other apart.

hard.hard: Lone pairs occupy space around the central atom and contribute to overall electron pair repulsion, just like bonding pairs, distorting what would otherwise be a linear or symmetric arrangement.
hard.medium: Oxygen has two extra pairs of electrons not involved in bonding, and these still push the hydrogen atoms out of a straight line.
hard.easy: Oxygen has two extra pairs of electrons that push the hydrogen atoms into a bent shape instead of a straight line.
